verdict: Caution on Chennai IT services lending: the data pack gives no score, and local news is of layoffs, so lend only to niche mid-tier firms with contracted order books and clean receivables; avoid body-shop staffing and single-client vendors.
title: Chennai Computer Software & IT: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
Pricing power belongs to firms with proprietary platforms or long-term managed-service contracts; pure staffing firms price-take and lose the first seat when a client cuts. The rating methodology flags exactly this: revenue is overseas, so US spend and visa norms drive collections [9], and working capital is the gap between receivables and payables [11]. ## What has changed now
**The local signal is layoffs, not growth: a Chennai delivery manager's anonymous account describes 12 people dismissed in 15 minutes, with no warnings [1][2].** That is unverified and company-unnamed, so treat it as sentiment, not a credit fact. The peer set is split: InfoBeans grew 22% in constant currency while giants stalled, but profit growth of 16% trailed revenue of 30% and 90-day receivables rose [4]; TCS held margins while its stock is down 30.3% year-to-date as AI erodes billable hours [5]; Sasken grew revenue 25.6% to Rs. 321 crores with software services up 34% and EBITDA margin up 700 basis points [7]. Cognizant's Q3 beat lifted the whole Nifty IT index nearly 2% [6]. So when a proposal lands, check which of these two profiles the borrower resembles; if revenue is growing but receivable days are stretching, ask why the cash is not following the invoice. ## Where the growth is
**Pursue Chennai firms riding the AI-infrastructure build-out: Vultr is unveiling India's largest AMD AI factory in Chennai on 2 November 2026 [3].** That pulls in sovereign-cloud and AI-compute services vendors, plus productised software firms with recurring licences. Pursue Sasken-type niche engineering-services exporters with 25.6% revenue growth and expanding margins [7], and mid-tier firms with 22%-type constant-currency growth and diversified clients [4]. Avoid pure bench-staffing vendors, single-client dependencies, and firms whose only differentiator is headcount. The rating criteria are blunt: geographic concentration in the US is a risk when spend slows [9]. ## How to grow safely
**Structure against the receivable, not the pitch.** Take monthly: ageing of receivables by client, billed-versus-unbilled revenue, top-five client concentration, attrition of billable staff, and monthly bank statements. Where receivables cross 90 days [4], convert part of the limit to a bill-discounted facility against confirmed invoices. Collect from customer: exact receivable days, client concentration percentages, and USD hedging policy, none of which the sources give.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch the payroll-to-collection gap first: salaries are fixed monthly, collections are not.** A borrower stretching payables while receivables age is funding operations from suppliers, and that ends badly. Second, watch senior attrition; the Chennai account shows middle managers absorbing decisions made above them [1], and departing delivery heads take client relationships. Third, watch a sudden shift from project to pure time-and-material billing, which is where AI pressure shows first [5]. The data pack carries no score for this sector, so the call rests on these fundamentals, not a number.
watch: Over 90 days on any single client -> shift that exposure to bill discounting and cap fresh limits
Above half of revenue in one client -> ask for contract tenure and add a client-diversification covenant
Delivery-head exits or bench rising -> freeze enhancement and re-check order book
Unbilled share climbing -> ask for milestone proof and reduce limit to billed book
Salary paid from overdraft rather than collections -> stop fresh disbursal and review
watch_note: Trigger levels are policy suggestions (analytical framing), not data.
news_why: Chennai layoff account and AI pressure on billable hours outweigh mixed peer results.
